title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
Motor insurers need to know whether poor portfolio results come from a broad deterioration or from a small number of identifiable risk segments. A single loss-ratio total is not sufficient because claim frequency, claim severity, exposure duration, policy design, customer loyalty, vehicle profile, and geography can all produce different underwriting implications.
This report uses visual analytics to investigate a Spanish motor insurance portfolio observed from 2022 to 2024. The analysis is framed as a mythbusting exercise: common stereotypes about insurance risk are tested against the data. The objective is not to build a pricing model. The objective is to discover which beliefs are supported by evidence, which are myths, and which are only partially true.



The analysis is organised around 10 research questions aligned with three strategic objectives:

Maximise overall portfolio profitability by identifying segments where loss ratio, claim frequency, claim severity, or underwriting result point to adverse performance.
Maximise retention and loyalty among low-risk, highly profitable customers by testing whether longer-observed customers and favourable behavioural signals are associated with better profitability.
Identify high-risk segments for appropriately calibrated premium pricing by separating stereotypes from evidence-backed signals that can support pricing, excess, coverage, renewal, or monitoring actions.

This makes the data wrangling purposeful: only variables needed to test a myth are retained, recoded, or derived. The guiding visual communication principle is one-look interpretation. Static charts, small multiples, and dashboards are preferred over animations because stakeholders should be able to compare segments without relying on memory.



Two source files are used:

data/Dataset of motor insurance portfolio.csv: policy-year motor insurance records.
data/Descriptive of variables.xlsx: variable descriptions and code definitions.

Each row is a policy-year observation. The same insured policy can appear in more than one year.

text:
2.1 R Packages
The package set is selected for reproducible data wrangling, static ggplot-based visual analytics, distribution-aware plots, and statistical validation.







Package
Purpose




tidyverse
Import, wrangling, plotting, and factor handling.


readxl
Import the Excel data dictionary.


knitr
Render compact summary tables.


scales
Format percentages, currency, and large numbers.


patchwork
Combine related plots into one-look dashboards.


ggdist
Half-eye and point-interval plots for distributions and uncertainty.


ggridges
Ridgeline density plots for ordered-group comparisons.


ggpubr
Statistical annotations on selected ggplot charts.


ggstatsplot
Statistical ggplot extensions such as ggbarstats() and ggbetweenstats().


viridis
Colour-blind-friendly palettes.


broom
Tidy statistical test results.





Show the code
pacman::p_load(
  tidyverse, readxl, knitr, scales,
  patchwork, ggdist, ggridges,
  ggpubr, ggstatsplot, viridis, broom
)

  detach("package:ggtern", unload = TRUE, character.only = TRUE)
}

theme_update(
  plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
  plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey35"),
  panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
  legend.position = "bottom",
  tern.axis.ticks.length.major = rel(0.5),
  tern.axis.ticks.length.minor = rel(0.25)
)

safe_divide <- function(numerator, denominator) {
  if_else(denominator > 0, numerator / denominator, NA_real_)
}

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
3.1 Visual Analytics Technique Selection Rationale
The visual analytics methods are selected to serve the three strategic objectives. The report therefore avoids using charts only because they are visually interesting. Each method is chosen because it answers a specific underwriting decision question.









Strategic objective
Analytical need
Technique selected
Rationale




Maximise portfolio profitability
Identify which segments are unprofitable and whether the issue is material
geom_tile() + geom_text() KPI matrices with break-even references where needed
Tile matrices make loss ratio, claim frequency, severity, and premium share comparable without using unsupported bar layers.


Maximise portfolio profitability
Diagnose whether poor results come from frequency, severity, or both
KPI matrices and stat_pointinterval()
These methods show frequency, severity, and uncertainty while staying inside the approved ggplot technique set.


Retain low-risk profitable customers
Compare loyalty groups and identify profitable retained segments
geom_tile() + geom_text() KPI matrices for loyalty_band and bonus score
KPI matrices connect retention directly to loss ratio and premium share, showing whether loyal customers are profitable enough to protect.


Retain low-risk profitable customers
Avoid blunt rules that penalise good customers inside broad segments
stat_halfeye() + geom_boxplot() + pairwise Wilcoxon or ggbetweenstats()
Distribution-aware plots show overlap within groups, preventing overconfidence in stereotypes such as age, bonus score, or brand status.


Calibrate premium pricing
Detect hidden tail-risk patterns in short exposure or claimant groups
geom_density_ridges_gradient() with quantile shading
Ridgelines compare distribution shape across ordered groups and reveal whether a segment has a heavier adverse tail rather than just a higher mean.


Calibrate premium pricing
Identify interaction risk that univariate charts may hide
geom_tile() heatmaps with embedded labels
Heatmaps make two-way combinations, such as driver age by vehicle age, readable at a glance and useful for pricing segmentation.


Calibrate premium pricing
Assess dense numerical signals such as power-to-weight
geom_hex() + geom_smooth(method = "gam")
Hexbin plots avoid overplotting in large policy-level data, while the GAM smoother shows whether a practical non-linear pattern exists.


Reproducibility and communication
Test categorical myths with statistical context
ggbarstats() and ggbetweenstats()
These approved ggplot extensions combine visual comparison with statistical evidence for categorical and numeric segment differences.



These choices also support the mythbusting structure. A myth is not confirmed by one chart alone; it is judged by the combined evidence of segment size, loss ratio, claim frequency, claim severity, and business relevance.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
4.2 Feature Selection and Recoding
Only variables needed for the 10 research questions are retained. Raw code values are recoded into stakeholder-readable labels.


Show the code
premium_brands <- c(
  "AUDI", "BMW", "FERRARI", "HUMMER", "INFINITI", "JAGUAR",
  "LAND ROVER", "LEXUS", "MASERATI", "MERCEDES", "MINI",
  "PORSCHE", "SAAB", "VOLVO"
)

portfolio <- portfolio_raw |>
  select(
    insured_id, year,
    policy_type, policy_status, business_type, payment_frequency, bonus_score,
    driver_age, vehicle_age, fuel_type, vehicle_value, power_to_weight_ratio,
    vehicle_brand, municipality_type, circulation_area,
    total_premium, total_claims, total_incurred, total_exposure
  ) |>
  mutate(
    policy_type = recode(
      policy_type,
      "TP" = "Third party",
      "TPG" = "Third party + glass",
      "CC" = "Third party + add-ons",
      "COMP_E" = "Comprehensive with excess",
      "COMP_N" = "Comprehensive without excess"
    ),
    policy_type = factor(
      policy_type,
      levels = c(
        "Third party", "Third party + glass", "Third party + add-ons",
        "Comprehensive with excess", "Comprehensive without excess"
      )
    ),
    policy_status = recode(policy_status, "A" = "Active", "C" = "Cancelled"),
    business_type = recode(business_type, "NB" = "New business", "P" = "Portfolio"),
    payment_frequency = recode(
      payment_frequency,
      "A" = "Annual", "S" = "Semiannual", "Q" = "Quarterly"
    ),
    bonus_score = recode(bonus_score, "G" = "Good", "N" = "Neutral", "B" = "Bad"),
    bonus_score = factor(bonus_score, levels = c("Good", "Neutral", "Bad")),
    fuel_type = recode(fuel_type, "D" = "Diesel", "G" = "Gasoline", .missing = "Unknown"),
    municipality_type = recode(
      municipality_type,
      "I" = "Inland", "C" = "Coastal", "IS" = "Islands"
    ),
    circulation_area = recode(circulation_area, "U" = "Urban", "R" = "Rural"),
    vehicle_brand = replace_na(vehicle_brand, "Unknown"),
    brand_tier = if_else(vehicle_brand %in% premium_brands, "Premium brand", "Mainstream brand"),
    geo_segment = str_c(municipality_type, " - ", circulation_area),
    across(
      c(
        policy_status, business_type, payment_frequency, fuel_type,
        municipality_type, circulation_area, vehicle_brand, brand_tier, geo_segment
      ),
      as_factor
    )
  )

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
4.3 Derived Analytical Variables
Loss ratio is used as the main profitability metric. Claim frequency and claim severity are separated because the underwriting action differs when a segment is high-frequency versus high-severity.


Show the code
portfolio <- portfolio |>
  mutate(
    loss_ratio = safe_divide(total_incurred, total_premium),
    underwriting_result = total_premium - total_incurred,
    claim_flag = total_claims > 0,
    claim_frequency = safe_divide(total_claims, total_exposure),
    claim_severity = safe_divide(total_incurred, total_claims),
    profit_status = case_when(
      total_claims == 0 ~ "No claim",
      loss_ratio <= 1 ~ "Claim, still profitable",
      TRUE ~ "Loss-making"
    ),
    profit_status = factor(
      profit_status,
      levels = c("Loss-making", "Claim, still profitable", "No claim")
    ),
    exposure_band = cut(
      total_exposure,
      breaks = c(0, 0.35, 0.75, 0.95, Inf),
      labels = c("Very short (<0.35)", "Short (0.35-0.75)", "Medium (0.75-0.95)", "Full (>0.95)"),
      include.lowest = TRUE
    ),
    driver_age_band = cut(
      driver_age,
      breaks = c(17, 25, 35, 45, 55, 65, Inf),
      labels = c("18-25", "26-35", "36-45", "46-55", "56-65", "66+"),
      right = TRUE
    ),
    vehicle_age_band = cut(
      vehicle_age,
      breaks = c(-Inf, 3, 7, 12, 20, Inf),
      labels = c("0-3", "4-7", "8-12", "13-20", "21+"),
      right = TRUE
    ),
    vehicle_value_band = ntile(vehicle_value, 5),
    vehicle_value_band = factor(
      vehicle_value_band,
      labels = c("Lowest", "Low", "Middle", "High", "Highest")
    ),
    same_insured_years = ave(
      year,
      insured_id,
      FUN = function(x) length(unique(x))
    ),
    loyalty_band = case_when(
      same_insured_years >= 3 ~ "Observed all 3 years",
      same_insured_years == 2 ~ "Observed 2 years",
      TRUE ~ "Observed 1 year"
    ),
    loyalty_band = factor(
      loyalty_band,
      levels = c("Observed 1 year", "Observed 2 years", "Observed all 3 years")
    )
  )

loss_ratio_cap_99 <- quantile(
  portfolio$loss_ratio[is.finite(portfolio$loss_ratio)],
  probs = 0.99,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

portfolio <- portfolio |>
  mutate(loss_ratio_capped_99 = pmin(loss_ratio, loss_ratio_cap_99))

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
4.4 Helper Summary Tables


Show the code
segment_summary <- function(data, segment_var) {
  data |>
    filter(!is.na({{ segment_var }})) |>
    group_by({{ segment_var }}) |>
    summarise(
      policies = n(),
      exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
      premium = sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
      claims = sum(total_claims, na.rm = TRUE),
      incurred = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE),
      underwriting_result = sum(underwriting_result, na.rm = TRUE),
      loss_ratio = incurred / premium,
      claim_frequency = claims / exposure,
      claim_severity = incurred / claims,
      claim_rate = mean(claim_flag, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    arrange(desc(premium))
}

portfolio_summary <- portfolio |>
  summarise(
    policy_years = n(),
    insured_policies = n_distinct(insured_id),
    exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    premium = sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
    claims = sum(total_claims, na.rm = TRUE),
    incurred = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE),
    underwriting_result = sum(underwriting_result, na.rm = TRUE),
    loss_ratio = incurred / premium,
    claim_frequency = claims / exposure,
    claim_severity = incurred / claims
  )

year_summary <- segment_summary(portfolio, year)
policy_type_summary <- segment_summary(portfolio, policy_type)
business_summary <- segment_summary(portfolio, business_type)
bonus_summary <- segment_summary(portfolio, bonus_score)
exposure_summary <- segment_summary(portfolio, exposure_band)
driver_age_summary <- segment_summary(portfolio, driver_age_band)

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
5.1 Portfolio at a Glance
Research questions supported: RQ1 and RQ2.
Technique justification: A patchwork dashboard combines the year trend, loss ratio, claim frequency, and underwriting result in one view. This is more intuitive than separate charts because the reader can immediately see whether deterioration is caused by loss ratio movement, claim frequency movement, or exposure scale.


Show the code
year_long <- year_summary |>
  select(year, premium, incurred, underwriting_result, loss_ratio, claim_frequency, exposure) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(premium, incurred, underwriting_result, loss_ratio, claim_frequency, exposure),
    names_to = "measure",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    measure = recode(
      measure,
      "premium" = "Premium",
      "incurred" = "Incurred loss",
      "underwriting_result" = "Underwriting result",
      "loss_ratio" = "Loss ratio",
      "claim_frequency" = "Claim frequency",
      "exposure" = "Exposure"
    ),
    label = case_when(
      measure %in% c("Loss ratio") ~ percent(value, accuracy = 0.1),
      measure %in% c("Claim frequency") ~ number(value, accuracy = 0.001),
      TRUE ~ label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())(value)
    )
  )

ggplot(year_long, aes(x = factor(year), y = measure, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), size = 3.2) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  labs(
    title = "Portfolio dashboard by year",
    subtitle = "Tile values keep profitability, frequency, materiality, and financial outcome visible at once",
    x = "Year",
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Value"
  )









What this tells us: The full 2022-2024 history is visible at once. The dashboard separates scale, profitability, and frequency so deterioration can be interpreted as a portfolio-management problem rather than as a single unexplained loss-ratio number.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
5.2 Executive Triage Map
Research questions supported: RQ1 and RQ2.
Technique justification: A KPI tile matrix replaces the earlier bubble map so the visual stays within the approved technique list. Claim frequency, claim severity, loss ratio, and premium share are shown together to preserve the triage logic.


Show the code

  mutate(
    metric = recode(
      metric,
      "loss_ratio" = "Loss ratio",
      "claim_frequency" = "Claim frequency",
      "claim_severity" = "Claim severity",
      "premium_share" = "Premium share"
    ),
    label = case_when(
      metric == "Claim severity" ~ dollar(value, prefix = ""),
      metric == "Claim frequency" ~ number(value, accuracy = 0.001),
      TRUE ~ percent(value, accuracy = 0.1)

  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  labs(
    title = "Policy-type triage: frequency, severity, profitability, materiality",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,

What this tells us: The chart separates frequency problems from severity problems. A policy type with high severity but low frequency needs a different response from a policy type with persistent high claim frequency.

text:
6.1 Portfolio Composition
Research questions supported: RQ1, RQ3, RQ4, RQ6, and RQ10.
Technique justification: ggbarstats() is used because it is one of the approved visual methods and it combines categorical composition with an association test. This makes the univariate-to-bivariate bridge explicit: policy type is shown together with profitability status.


Show the code
ggbarstats(
  data = portfolio,
  x = policy_type,
  y = profit_status,
  label = "percentage",
  results.subtitle = FALSE,
  title = "Policy type composition by profitability status",

  legend.title = "Profitability status"
) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = 1))









What this tells us: The portfolio is not evenly distributed across segments. This matters because a high loss ratio in a tiny segment should not be interpreted the same way as a moderate loss ratio in a large premium segment.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
6.2 Numerical Feature Distributions
Research questions supported: RQ7, RQ8, and RQ9.
Technique justification: Histograms with free scales show the empirical shape of numeric risk features. Vehicle value is shown on a log scale because the distribution is strongly right-skewed.


Show the code
numeric_long <- portfolio |>
  transmute(
    `Driver age` = driver_age,
    `Vehicle age` = vehicle_age,
    `Power-to-weight ratio` = power_to_weight_ratio,
    `Vehicle value` = vehicle_value
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "feature", values_to = "value") |>
  filter(!is.na(value), value > 0)

ggplot(numeric_long, aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 35, fill = "#4C78A8", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ feature, scales = "free", ncol = 2) +

  labs(
    title = "Distribution of continuous risk features",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Policy-year records"
  )









What this tells us: Vehicle value and power-to-weight are skewed, so later charts use log scales, hexbin density, or capped outcome variables rather than relying on raw scatterplots.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
section: 7.1 RQ1: Are Younger Drivers Genuinely Less Profitable Than Older Drivers?
text:
7.1 RQ1: Are Younger Drivers Genuinely Less Profitable Than Older Drivers?
Myth tested: Young drivers are always the worst risks.
Technique justification: A two-panel KPI chart bridges univariate and bivariate analysis: the first panel shows premium materiality by age band, while the second panel compares loss ratio and claim frequency. This prevents overreacting to a small segment that has high frequency but limited portfolio weight.


Show the code
driver_kpi_long <- driver_age_summary |>
  select(driver_age_band, share_premium = premium, loss_ratio, claim_frequency) |>
  mutate(share_premium = share_premium / sum(share_premium)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(share_premium, loss_ratio, claim_frequency),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    metric = recode(
      metric,
      "share_premium" = "Premium share",
      "loss_ratio" = "Loss ratio",
      "claim_frequency" = "Claim frequency"
    )
  )

ggplot(driver_kpi_long, aes(metric, driver_age_band, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = if_else(metric == "Claim frequency", number(value, accuracy = 0.001), percent(value, accuracy = 0.1))),
    size = 3
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", labels = label_number()) +
  labs(
    title = "Driver age myth check: frequency is not the same as profitability",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Driver age band",
    fill = "Value"
  )









What this tells us: The stereotype is mixed. Drivers aged 18-25 have the highest claim frequency (0.488), but their loss ratio is only 62.5% and they contribute just 1.0% of premium. The highest age-band loss ratio belongs to 26-35 at 73.3%.

section: 7.2 RQ2: Does Vehicle Age Increase Loss Ratio and Claim Frequency?
text:
7.2 RQ2: Does Vehicle Age Increase Loss Ratio and Claim Frequency?
Myth tested: Older vehicles are always riskier.
Technique justification: Ranked KPI bars are used because the myth has two different dimensions: frequency and profitability. The chart shows whether the same vehicle-age band is worst on both.


Show the code
vehicle_age_long <- vehicle_age_summary |>
  select(vehicle_age_band, loss_ratio, claim_frequency, claim_severity) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(loss_ratio, claim_frequency, claim_severity),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    metric = recode(
      metric,
      "loss_ratio" = "Loss ratio",
      "claim_frequency" = "Claim frequency",
      "claim_severity" = "Claim severity"
    )
  )

ggplot(vehicle_age_long, aes(metric, vehicle_age_band, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = case_when(
      metric == "Claim severity" ~ dollar(value, prefix = ""),
      metric == "Claim frequency" ~ number(value, accuracy = 0.001),
      TRUE ~ percent(value, accuracy = 0.1)
    )),
    size = 3

What this tells us: The stereotype is partly real but incomplete. Vehicles aged 0-3 have the highest claim frequency at 0.524, but the weakest loss ratio is 13-20 at 75.2%. Very old vehicles aged 21+ are more profitable than the stereotype suggests.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
section: 7.3 RQ3: Which Policy Types Create the Most Profitability Pressure?
text:
7.3 RQ3: Which Policy Types Create the Most Profitability Pressure?
Myth tested: Comprehensive policies are safer because customers pay more.
Technique justification: A ranked loss-ratio bar with a break-even line is used because policy type is a compact product-design variable and the strategic action depends on whether the segment approaches or exceeds 100%.


Show the code
ggplot(
  policy_type_summary,
  aes(x = "Loss ratio", y = fct_reorder(policy_type, loss_ratio), fill = loss_ratio)
) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(loss_ratio, accuracy = 0.1)), size = 3.4) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1), option = "C") +
  labs(
    title = "Policy type myth check: higher cover does not guarantee stronger profitability",
    subtitle = "Break-even reference is 100%; darker cells indicate higher loss ratio",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Loss ratio"
  )









What this tells us: The myth is busted. Comprehensive without excess has the weakest loss ratio at 93.9% and the highest claim frequency at 1.046. Premium adequacy and excess design need review.

7.4 RQ4: Are Premium Vehicle Brands Less Profitable Than Mainstream Brands?
Myth tested: Premium brands are the biggest loss drivers.
Technique justification: A brand-tier KPI chart is used before brand-level analysis because it tests the status stereotype directly. It compares premium share, loss ratio, claim frequency, and severity in one readable view.


Show the code
brand_kpi_long <- brand_tier_summary |>
  select(brand_tier, premium, loss_ratio, claim_frequency, claim_severity) |>
  mutate(premium_share = premium / sum(premium)) |>

  pivot_longer(-brand_tier, names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(
    metric = recode(
      metric,
      "premium_share" = "Premium share",
      "loss_ratio" = "Loss ratio",
      "claim_frequency" = "Claim frequency",
      "claim_severity" = "Claim severity"
    )
  )

ggplot(brand_kpi_long, aes(metric, brand_tier, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = case_when(
      metric == "Claim severity" ~ dollar(value, prefix = ""),
      metric == "Claim frequency" ~ number(value, accuracy = 0.001),
      TRUE ~ percent(value, accuracy = 0.1)
    )),

  labs(
    title = "Brand prestige myth check",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Value"
  )









What this tells us: The myth is mostly busted. Premium brands have higher claim frequency (0.403) than mainstream brands, but their loss ratio is lower at 68.9% versus 70.7%. Premium brand status is a frequency signal, not the main profitability drain.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
section: 7.5 RQ5: Does Vehicle Value Show a Monotonic Relationship With Loss Ratio?
text:
7.5 RQ5: Does Vehicle Value Show a Monotonic Relationship With Loss Ratio?
Myth tested: Higher vehicle value always means poorer profitability.
Technique justification: Ordered bars by vehicle-value quintile show whether profitability worsens steadily with value. This is more direct than a scatterplot because the pricing question is about segment-level calibration.


Show the code
value_long <- vehicle_value_summary |>
  select(vehicle_value_band, loss_ratio, claim_frequency) |>
  pivot_longer(-vehicle_value_band, names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(metric = recode(metric, "loss_ratio" = "Loss ratio", "claim_frequency" = "Claim frequency"))

ggplot(value_long, aes(metric, vehicle_value_band, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = if_else(metric == "Claim frequency", number(value, accuracy = 0.001), percent(value, accuracy = 0.1))),
    size = 3.1
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", labels = label_number()) +
  labs(
    title = "Vehicle value myth check: the pattern is not monotonic",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Vehicle value quintile",
    fill = "Value"
  )









What this tells us: The myth is mixed. The highest-value band has high claim frequency (0.410) and a loss ratio of 73.3%, but the lowest-value band is also weak at 72.3%. Vehicle value should calibrate severity assumptions, not be treated as a one-direction rule.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
section: 7.6 RQ6: Does Bonus Score Separate Profitable and Unprofitable Customers?
text:
7.6 RQ6: Does Bonus Score Separate Profitable and Unprofitable Customers?
Myth tested: Bad bonus-score customers are always the worst.
Technique justification: stat_halfeye() shows distribution shape, geom_boxplot() shows compact spread, and pairwise Wilcoxon tests provide non-parametric evidence for differences across bonus-score groups.


Show the code
ggplot(
  portfolio |> filter(!is.na(bonus_score), loss_ratio_capped_99 > 0),
  aes(x = bonus_score, y = loss_ratio_capped_99, fill = bonus_score)
) +
  stat_halfeye(
    adjust = 0.8, 
    width = 0.55, 
    justification = -0.2, 
    .width = 0, 
    alpha = 0.65, 
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.16, 
    outlier.shape = NA, 
    alpha = 0.5, 
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_jitter(
    width = 0.08, 
    alpha = 0.03, 
    size = 0.35, 
    show.legend = FALSE,
    color = "#2C3E50" 
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#C0392B", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = number_format(accuracy = 0.1)) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(
    title = "Bonus Score Myth Check: Claim Severity",
    subtitle = "Distribution of loss ratios (excluding zero-claim policies); dashed line = break-even",
    x = "Bonus Score",
    y = "Loss Ratio (Capped at 99th percentile)"
  )











Show the code
pairwise.wilcox.test(
  x = portfolio$loss_ratio_capped_99,
  g = portfolio$bonus_score,
  p.adjust.method = "holm"
)$p.value |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("Comparison") |>
  kable(digits = 4)

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
section: 7.7 RQ7: Are Short-Exposure Policies a Hidden Profitability Problem?
text:
7.7 RQ7: Are Short-Exposure Policies a Hidden Profitability Problem?
Myth tested: Short-term policies are harmless because exposure is small.
Technique justification: geom_density_ridges_gradient() with quantile shading compares ordered exposure-duration distributions. This is better than a mean-only chart because the myth concerns hidden tail risk.


Show the code
ggplot(
  portfolio |> filter(claim_flag, !is.na(exposure_band), !is.na(loss_ratio_capped_99)),
  aes(x = loss_ratio_capped_99, y = exposure_band, fill = factor(after_stat(quantile)))
) +
  geom_density_ridges_gradient(
    calc_ecdf = TRUE,
    quantiles = 4,
    quantile_lines = TRUE,
    scale = 1.8,
    rel_min_height = 0.005
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "Quartile", option = "C") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = number_format(accuracy = 0.1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Exposure-duration myth check",
    subtitle = "Claimants only; dashed line = break-even",
    x = "Loss ratio capped at 99th percentile",
    y = "Exposure band"
  ) +
  theme_ridges(font_size = 11, grid = TRUE)









What this tells us: The myth is busted. Very short policies have a loss ratio of 103.3%, the only exposure band above break-even. Although they contribute only 4.5% of premium, they are a strong quality-monitoring signal.

7.8 RQ8: Are Longer-Observed Customers More Profitable and Worth Retaining?
Myth tested: Loyal customers are just retained volume, not necessarily profitable.
Technique justification: A loyalty-band KPI chart compares premium share, loss ratio, and cancellation rate. This directly links retention strategy to profitability, rather than treating loyalty as a volume metric only.


Show the code
loyalty_long <- loyalty_summary |>
  select(loyalty_band, premium, loss_ratio, claim_frequency, cancel_rate = claim_rate) |>
  mutate(premium_share = premium / sum(premium)) |>
  select(loyalty_band, premium_share, loss_ratio, claim_frequency) |>
  pivot_longer(-loyalty_band, names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(
    metric = recode(
      metric,
      "premium_share" = "Premium share",
      "loss_ratio" = "Loss ratio",
      "claim_frequency" = "Claim frequency"
    )
  )

ggplot(loyalty_long, aes(metric, loyalty_band, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = if_else(metric == "Claim frequency", number(value, accuracy = 0.001), percent(value, accuracy = 0.1))),
    size = 3
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", labels = label_number()) +
  labs(
    title = "Loyalty myth check: retained customers are materially more profitable",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Observed policy years in dataset",
    fill = "Value"
  )









What this tells us: The myth is busted. Customers observed all 3 years have the best loss ratio at 63.4% and contribute 52.2% of premium. Retaining stable low-risk customers is directly aligned with profitability.


Show the code
set.seed(608)
loyalty_between_data <- portfolio |>
  filter(!is.na(loyalty_band), !is.na(loss_ratio_capped_99))

loyalty_between_data <- loyalty_between_data |>

ggbetweenstats(

  xlab = "Observed policy years in dataset",
  ylab = "Loss ratio capped at 99th percentile"
)

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
section: 7.9 RQ9: Are Cancelled Policies Actually Worse Risks Than Active Policies?
text:
7.9 RQ9: Are Cancelled Policies Actually Worse Risks Than Active Policies?
Myth tested: Cancelled policies are removed risks, so cancellation is good.
Technique justification: A status KPI chart compares active and cancelled policies across loss ratio, frequency, severity, and premium share. This tests whether cancellation is associated with risk quality or just administrative status.


Show the code
status_summary <- segment_summary(portfolio, policy_status)

status_long <- status_summary |>
  select(policy_status, premium, loss_ratio, claim_frequency, claim_severity) |>
  mutate(premium_share = premium / sum(premium)) |>
  select(policy_status, premium_share, loss_ratio, claim_frequency, claim_severity) |>
  pivot_longer(-policy_status, names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(
    metric = recode(
      metric,
      "premium_share" = "Premium share",
      "loss_ratio" = "Loss ratio",
      "claim_frequency" = "Claim frequency",
      "claim_severity" = "Claim severity"
    )
  )

ggplot(status_long, aes(metric, policy_status, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = case_when(
      metric == "Claim severity" ~ dollar(value, prefix = ""),
      metric == "Claim frequency" ~ number(value, accuracy = 0.001),
      TRUE ~ percent(value, accuracy = 0.1)
    )),
    size = 3
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", labels = label_number()) +
  labs(
    title = "Cancellation myth check",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Policy status",
    fill = "Value"
  )









What this tells us: The myth is real, but operationally important. Cancelled policies have a loss ratio of 128.0% versus 64.4% for active policies. The insurer should identify these risks earlier, not only after cancellation has occurred.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
section: 7.10 RQ10: Does Geography Materially Affect Frequency, Severity, and Loss Ratio?
text:
7.10 RQ10: Does Geography Materially Affect Frequency, Severity, and Loss Ratio?
Myth tested: Urban areas are always worse than rural areas.
Technique justification: Geography is assessed with circulation-area bars and geo-segment intervals. This separates frequency-driven urban risk from severity-driven rural risk.


Show the code
area_summary <- segment_summary(portfolio, circulation_area)

area_long <- area_summary |>
  select(circulation_area, loss_ratio, claim_frequency, claim_severity) |>
  pivot_longer(-circulation_area, names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(
    metric = recode(
      metric,
      "loss_ratio" = "Loss ratio",
      "claim_frequency" = "Claim frequency",
      "claim_severity" = "Claim severity"
    )
  )

ggplot(area_long, aes(metric, circulation_area, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = case_when(
      metric == "Claim severity" ~ dollar(value, prefix = ""),
      metric == "Claim frequency" ~ number(value, accuracy = 0.001),
      TRUE ~ percent(value, accuracy = 0.1)
    )),
    size = 3.1
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", labels = label_number()) +
  labs(
    title = "Urban-rural myth check",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Circulation area",
    fill = "Value"
  )









What this tells us: The myth is mostly real for frequency but mixed for severity. Urban policies have higher claim frequency (0.335) and loss ratio (71.4%), while rural policies have higher severity (995.91). Urban pricing should focus on frequency; rural review should pay attention to severity.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
section: 8.1 Which Driver-Age and Vehicle-Age Combinations Elevate Claim Risk?
text:
8.1 Which Driver-Age and Vehicle-Age Combinations Elevate Claim Risk?
Research question: Which driver-age and vehicle-age combinations elevate claim risk?
Technique justification: A heatmap is the most compact way to show a two-way interaction. Embedded labels make the answer readable without requiring the viewer to inspect a colour legend alone.


Show the code
age_heatmap <- portfolio |>
  filter(!is.na(driver_age_band), !is.na(vehicle_age_band)) |>
  group_by(driver_age_band, vehicle_age_band) |>
  summarise(
    exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    claims = sum(total_claims, na.rm = TRUE),
    claim_frequency = claims / exposure,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(age_heatmap, aes(vehicle_age_band, driver_age_band, fill = claim_frequency)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = number(claim_frequency, accuracy = 0.01)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", labels = number_format(accuracy = 0.01)) +
  labs(
    title = "Claim frequency by driver age and vehicle age",
    x = "Vehicle age band",
    y = "Driver age band",
    fill = "Claim frequency"
  )









What this tells us: The interaction view identifies combinations that can be missed when driver age and vehicle age are analysed separately. These cells are candidates for refined underwriting rules or pricing interactions.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
section: 8.2 Do Brand, Value, and Power-to-Weight Signals Identify Severity Risk?
text:
8.2 Do Brand, Value, and Power-to-Weight Signals Identify Severity Risk?
Research question: Do brand, value, and power-to-weight signals identify severity risk?
Technique justification: A point-interval chart compares brand tiers with uncertainty, while a hexbin plus GAM smoother handles dense policy-level numeric data without overplotting.


Show the code
p_brand_tier <- ggplot(
  portfolio |>
    filter(claim_flag, !is.na(brand_tier), !is.na(claim_severity), claim_severity > 0),
  aes(x = brand_tier, y = claim_severity)
) +
  stat_pointinterval(
    .width = c(0.8, 0.95),
    point_size = 3,
    aes(colour = factor(after_stat(.width)))
  ) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = dollar_format(prefix = "")) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("0.8" = "#4C78A8", "0.95" = "#F58518"),
    labels = c("80% interval", "95% interval"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  labs(title = "Claim severity by brand tier", x = NULL, y = "Claim severity")

p_power <- ggplot(
  portfolio |>
    filter(
      !is.na(power_to_weight_ratio),
      !is.na(loss_ratio_capped_99),
      power_to_weight_ratio > 0
    ),
  aes(power_to_weight_ratio, loss_ratio_capped_99)
) +
  geom_hex(bins = 35) +
  geom_smooth(method = "gam", formula = y ~ s(x, bs = "cs"), colour = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(labels = comma, option = "C") +
  labs(
    title = "Power-to-weight versus loss ratio",
    x = "Power-to-weight ratio",
    y = "Loss ratio",
    fill = "Records"
  )

p_brand_tier | p_power









What this tells us: Brand and vehicle-performance signals should be treated as severity or tail-risk indicators only if they show visible separation after considering uncertainty and dense-record patterns.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
section: 8.3 Which Segments Should Be Reviewed First?
text:
8.3 Which Segments Should Be Reviewed First?
Research questions supported: RQ1 to RQ10.
Technique justification: A priority table turns the visual findings into an action queue. It combines loss ratio, frequency, severity, premium materiality, and evidence strength so the report ends with a decision-oriented output.


Show the code
priority_tbl <- bind_rows(
  policy_type_summary |> transmute(segment_type = "Policy type", segment = as.character(policy_type), premium, loss_ratio, claim_frequency, claim_severity),
  segment_summary(portfolio, policy_status) |> transmute(segment_type = "Policy status", segment = as.character(policy_status), premium, loss_ratio, claim_frequency, claim_severity),
  bonus_summary |> transmute(segment_type = "Bonus score", segment = as.character(bonus_score), premium, loss_ratio, claim_frequency, claim_severity),
  exposure_summary |> transmute(segment_type = "Exposure band", segment = as.character(exposure_band), premium, loss_ratio, claim_frequency, claim_severity),
  driver_age_summary |> transmute(segment_type = "Driver age", segment = as.character(driver_age_band), premium, loss_ratio, claim_frequency, claim_severity),
  vehicle_age_summary |> transmute(segment_type = "Vehicle age", segment = as.character(vehicle_age_band), premium, loss_ratio, claim_frequency, claim_severity),
  vehicle_value_summary |> transmute(segment_type = "Vehicle value", segment = as.character(vehicle_value_band), premium, loss_ratio, claim_frequency, claim_severity),
  brand_tier_summary |> transmute(segment_type = "Brand tier", segment = as.character(brand_tier), premium, loss_ratio, claim_frequency, claim_severity),
  loyalty_summary |> transmute(segment_type = "Loyalty", segment = as.character(loyalty_band), premium, loss_ratio, claim_frequency, claim_severity),
  geo_summary |> transmute(segment_type = "Geography", segment = as.character(geo_segment), premium, loss_ratio, claim_frequency, claim_severity)
) |>
  filter(!is.na(segment), premium > 0) |>
  mutate(
    materiality_score = percent_rank(premium),
    loss_score = percent_rank(loss_ratio),
    frequency_score = percent_rank(claim_frequency),
    severity_score = percent_rank(replace_na(claim_severity, 0)),
    priority_score = 0.35 * loss_score + 0.25 * frequency_score +
      0.20 * severity_score + 0.20 * materiality_score
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(priority_score)) |>
  slice_head(n = 12)

priority_tbl |>
  transmute(
    Rank = row_number(),
    `Segment type` = segment_type,
    Segment = segment,
    Premium = dollar(premium, prefix = ""),
    `Loss ratio` = percent(loss_ratio, accuracy = 0.1),
    `Claim frequency` = number(claim_frequency, accuracy = 0.001),
    `Claim severity` = dollar(claim_severity, prefix = ""),
    `Priority score` = number(priority_score, accuracy = 0.01)
  ) |>
  kable()

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
8.4 Statistical Validation
Technique justification: Statistical tests are used as directional validation, not as a replacement for visual interpretation. With a large dataset, very small differences can become statistically significant, so practical significance still depends on visual effect size and premium exposure.


Show the code
kw_test <- function(variable) {
  formula <- as.formula(str_c("loss_ratio_capped_99 ~ ", variable))
  kruskal.test(formula, data = portfolio) |>
    tidy() |>
    mutate(test = "Kruskal-Wallis", variable = variable)
}

chisq_test <- function(variable) {
  tbl <- table(portfolio[[variable]], portfolio$claim_flag)
  chisq.test(tbl) |>
    tidy() |>
    mutate(test = "Chi-square", variable = variable)
}

spearman_test <- function(variable) {
  cor.test(
    portfolio[[variable]],
    portfolio$loss_ratio_capped_99,
    method = "spearman",
    exact = FALSE
  ) |>
    tidy() |>
    mutate(test = "Spearman", variable = variable)
}

validation_tbl <- bind_rows(
  map_dfr(
    c("policy_type", "business_type", "policy_status", "bonus_score",
      "exposure_band", "driver_age_band", "vehicle_age_band", "vehicle_value_band",
      "brand_tier", "loyalty_band", "geo_segment"),
    kw_test
  ),
  map_dfr(
    c("policy_type", "business_type", "policy_status", "bonus_score",
      "exposure_band", "driver_age_band", "vehicle_age_band", "vehicle_value_band",
      "brand_tier", "loyalty_band", "geo_segment"),
    chisq_test
  ),
  map_dfr(
    c("driver_age", "vehicle_age", "vehicle_value", "power_to_weight_ratio"),
    spearman_test
  )
) |>
  transmute(
    test,
    variable,
    statistic = round(statistic, 3),
    estimate = round(estimate, 3),
    p_value = p.value
  ) |>
  arrange(p_value)

validation_tbl |>
  mutate(p_value = pvalue(p_value, accuracy = 0.001)) |>
  kable()

title: Hands-on Exercise 8:
text:
This hands-on exercise follows Chapter 17: Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data from R for Visual Analytics. Rather than reproducing the reference work line-for-line, I rebuild each technique with my own variations (different focal series, colour systems, faceting and themes) and then add an Extras section with five pieces of analysis that appear in neither the chapter nor the reference notebook.
The techniques covered are:

plotting a calendar heatmap with ggplot2 (my version uses a viridis colour scale and a Monday-first weekday order),
plotting a cycle plot (my version profiles Japan over the full 2000-2019 window),
plotting a slopegraph with CGPfunctions (my version contrasts 1980 vs 2010 and highlights the biggest movers),
plus five extras: a horizon chart, a 24-hour radial attack clock, a GitHub-style calendar grid, a gridExtra side-by-side comparison, and a rice-yield growth ranking.


Scope rule. I only use packages that already appear in the source chapter or the reference notebook. The union of those two package lists is the full toolbox below - nothing else is introduced. Note that viridis, gridExtra and data.table are loaded by the reference but never actually used there; my variations and extras put them to work. ggHoriPlot is listed by the source chapter but not used by either file, so the horizon chart in Section 6 is built strictly within the allowed toolbox.

title: Hands-on Exercise 8:
text:
3.2 Data preparation
Like the reference, I convert each UTC timestamp to its local time before pulling out the weekday and hour, because the source country’s tile only makes sense in local time. My variation differs in two ways:

I replace the superseded do() + helper-function pattern with a modern group_modify() over each timezone, and
I derive the weekday with lubridate::wday(week_start = 1) mapped to fixed English labels (locale-independent), ordering the axis Monday at the top instead of the reference’s Saturday-first order.


wkday_levels <- c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday",
                  "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday")

attacks_cleaned <- attacks %>%
  group_by(tz) %>%
  group_modify(~ {
    local_times <- ymd_hms(.x$timestamp) %>% with_tz(tzone = .y$tz)
    tibble(
      source_country = .x$source_country,

The reference compares 1961 vs 1980. My variation compares the most recent 30-year span in the data, 1980 vs 2010, and instead of colouring every country I grey out the field and highlight the two steepest climbers (Vietnam and Myanmar) with newggslopegraph()’s named LineColor argument.

rice_years <- rice %>%

                  SubTitle = "Vietnam and Myanmar posted the steepest gains over the period",

Horizon chart of air arrivals (ggHoriPlot)
ggHoriPlot is listed by the source chapter’s package set but neither file builds a horizon chart. A horizon plot folds a series into stacked, colour-banded layers so many time series can be compared in a compact strip. Here I profile monthly arrivals for six markets across 2000-2019.

arrivals_long <- air %>%
  select(`Month-Year`, China, Japan, `South Korea`, USA, Australia, India) %>%
  pivot_longer(-`Month-Year`, names_to = "country", values_to = "arrivals") %>%
  mutate(date = as.Date(`Month-Year`))

p_horizon <- ggplot(arrivals_long) +
  geom_horizon(aes(date, arrivals, fill = after_stat(Cutpoints)),
               origin = "midpoint", horizonscale = 6) +
  scale_fill_hcl(palette = "RdBu", reverse = TRUE) +
  facet_grid(country ~ .) +
  theme_few() +
  scale_x_date(expand = c(0, 0), date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(title = "Monthly visitor arrivals by air, 2000-2019",
       subtitle = "Horizon bands: blue = below the series midpoint, red = above",
       x = NULL) +
  theme(panel.spacing.y = unit(0, "lines"),
        strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0, size = 8),
        axis.text.y  = element_blank(),
        axis.title.y = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
        panel.border = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none",
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 8))

A 24-hour radial “attack clock” (coord_polar)
The Section 3 heatmap reads time on a Cartesian axis. Wrapping the hour-of-day totals around coord_polar() turns them into a clock face, making the daily rhythm of attacks immediately legible.

hourly <- attacks_cleaned %>%

p_clock <- ggplot(hourly, aes(x = hour, y = n, fill = n)) +
  geom_col(width = 1, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  coord_polar(start = 0) +
  scale_fill_viridis(name = "# of attacks", option = "magma", direction = -1) +
  labs(title = "A 24-hour clock of attack volume",
       subtitle = "Each wedge is one hour of the day (local time)",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Helvetica") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),

title: Hands-on Exercise 8:
text:
GitHub-style calendar grid heatmap (lubridate + viridis)
The reference “calendar heatmap” is really a weekday-by-hour grid. Here I build a true calendar layout: one panel per month, weekdays across the columns and week-of-month down the rows, each day-cell shaded by its total attack count - exactly the layout GitHub uses for contribution graphs.

daily <- attacks %>%
  mutate(date = as_date(ymd_hms(timestamp))) %>%
  count(date) %>%
  mutate(
    month         = month(date, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE),
    wday          = wday(date, week_start = 1),                # 1 = Mon ... 7 = Sun
    first_wday    = wday(floor_date(date, "month"), week_start = 1),
    week_of_month = ceiling((day(date) + first_wday - 1) / 7)
  )

p_calendar <- ggplot(daily, aes(x = wday, y = week_of_month, fill = n)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ month, ncol = 4) +
  scale_y_reverse(breaks = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:7,
                     labels = c("M", "T", "W", "T", "F", "S", "S")) +
  scale_fill_viridis(name = "attacks/day", option = "viridis", direction = -1) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Daily attack counts laid out as a calendar (2015)",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Helvetica") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))

ggsave("images/extra_calendar_grid.png", p_calendar, width = 9, height = 5, dpi = 150)
p_calendar

title: Hands-on Exercise 8:
text:
Side-by-side cycle plots (gridExtra::grid.arrange)
gridExtra is loaded by both reference files but never used. I put it to work to stack two cycle plots into a single comparison panel - here South Korea vs China arrivals from 2010 - so their seasonal shapes can be read against each other.

cycle_plot <- function(df, country) {
  d <- df %>%
    transmute(month, year, value = .data[[country]]) %>%
    filter(year >= 2010)
  hl <- d %>% group_by(month) %>% summarise(avgvalue = mean(value))

  ggplot() +
    geom_line(data = d, aes(year, value, group = month),
              colour = "grey25", linewidth = 0.4) +
    geom_hline(data = hl, aes(yintercept = avgvalue),
               colour = "firebrick", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
    facet_grid(~ month) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
    labs(title = country, x = NULL, y = "Visitors") +
    theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
          axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
          plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 11),
          strip.text = element_text(size = 7))
}

p_kr <- cycle_plot(air, "South Korea")
p_cn <- cycle_plot(air, "China")

p_compare <- arrangeGrob(p_kr, p_cn, ncol = 1,
                         top = "Cycle plots compared: South Korea vs China, 2010-2019")
ggsave("images/extra_cycle_compare.png", p_compare, width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 150)
grid.arrange(p_compare)

title: Hands-on Exercise 8:
text:
Rice-yield growth ranking (scales::percent)
The slopegraph shows two endpoints; this extra distils the whole story into a ranking. I compute each country’s percentage change in rice yield from 1961 to 2010 and draw a lollipop chart sorted by growth, labelled with scales::percent().

rice_growth <- rice %>%
  filter(Year %in% c(1961, 2010)) %>%
  select(Country, Year, Yield) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Year, values_from = Yield, names_prefix = "y") %>%
  mutate(growth = (y2010 - y1961) / y1961) %>%
  arrange(growth) %>%
  mutate(Country = factor(Country, levels = Country))

p_growth <- ggplot(rice_growth, aes(x = growth, y = Country)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = growth, y = Country, yend = Country),
               colour = "grey75") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = growth), size = 4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(growth, accuracy = 1)),
            hjust = -0.25, size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.18))) +
  scale_colour_viridis(option = "D", guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Growth in rice yield, 1961 to 2010",
       subtitle = "Percentage change in yield (kg/ha) per country",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Helvetica") +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 8))

ggsave("images/extra_yield_growth.png", p_growth, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 150)
p_growth

title: Hands-on Exercise 7-A:
text:
This hands-on exercise covers Chapter 27: Modelling, Visualising and Analysing Network Data with R.
By the end of this exercise, I will be able to:

create graph object data frames, manipulate them using appropriate functions of dplyr, lubridate, and tidygraph,
build network graph visualisation using appropriate functions of ggraph,
compute network geometrics using tidygraph,
build advanced graph visualisation by incorporating the network geometrics, and
build interactive network visualisation using visNetwork package.

title: Hands-on Exercise 7-A:
text:
2.1 Loading the required packages
For this exercise we will use the following R packages:

igraph, tidygraph, ggraph and visNetwork for modelling and visualising network data,
graphlayouts for additional network layouts,
lubridate and clock for wrangling dates and times,
concaveman and ggforce for drawing community hulls,
DT for interactive tables (used in the Extras), and
tidyverse for general data wrangling and plotting.


pacman::p_load(igraph, tidygraph, ggraph,
               visNetwork, lubridate, clock,
               tidyverse, graphlayouts,
               concaveman, ggforce, DT)

title: Hands-on Exercise 7-A:
text:
4.1 The tbl_graph object
Two functions of tidygraph can be used to create network objects:

tbl_graph() creates a tbl_graph network object from nodes and edges data.
as_tbl_graph() converts network data and objects (igraph, network, data.frame, dendrogram, etc.) into a tbl_graph network.

title: Hands-on Exercise 7-A:
text:
4.2 The dplyr verbs in tidygraph

activate() serves as a switch between the tibbles for nodes and edges. All dplyr verbs applied to a tbl_graph object are applied to the active tibble.



.N() gives access to the node data while manipulating edge data. Similarly .E() gives the edge data and .G() gives the tbl_graph object itself.

                           edges = GAStech_edges_aggregated,
                           directed = TRUE)

This is a directed graph, so the direction of the messages is relevant.

title: Hands-on Exercise 7-A:
text:
7.1 Computing centrality indices
Centrality measures are a collection of statistical indices used to describe the relative importance of the actors in a network. Four well-known measures are: degree, betweenness, closeness and eigenvector.

g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  mutate(betweenness_centrality = centrality_betweenness()) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = Weight),
                 alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department,
                      size = betweenness_centrality))
g + theme_graph()

title: Hands-on Exercise 7-A:
text:
7.2 Visualising network metrics
From ggraph v2.0 onward, the centrality measure can be computed directly inside aes(), without pre-computing a column.

g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = Weight),
                 alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department,
                      size = centrality_betweenness()))
g + theme_graph()

title: Hands-on Exercise 7-A:
text:
7.3 Visualising Community
Communities are groups of nodes that are closely knit. The measure of being closely knit is the Weight column in our graph.
Reference: https://towardsdatascience.com/community-detection-algorithms-9bd8951e7dae

g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  mutate(community = as.factor(
    group_edge_betweenness(
      weights = Weight,
      directed = TRUE))) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = Weight),
                 alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = community))

g + theme_graph()









7.3.1 Marking communities with hulls
The most recent version of the chapter adds an advanced community visualisation that draws a hull around each community using geom_mark_hull() of ggforce (which relies on concaveman). Communities are detected here with group_optimal() and node size is scaled by betweenness.

g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  activate(nodes) %>%
  mutate(community = as.factor(group_optimal(weights = Weight)),
         betweenness_measure = centrality_betweenness()) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_mark_hull(
    aes(x, y,
        group = community,
        fill = community),
    alpha = 0.2,
    expand = unit(0.3, "cm"),
    radius = unit(0.3, "cm")
  ) +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = Weight),
                 alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(fill = Department,
                      size = betweenness_measure),
                  color = "black",
                  shape = 21)

g + theme_graph()

title: Hands-on Exercise 7-A:
text:
8.1 Data preparation
Before plotting the interactive graph, we prepare a data model whose edges reference the node ids. We join the edge and node data frames to recover the from/to ids from the labels.

GAStech_edges_aggregated <- GAStech_edges %>%
  left_join(GAStech_nodes, by = c("sourceLabel" = "label")) %>%
  rename(from = id) %>%
  left_join(GAStech_nodes, by = c("targetLabel" = "label")) %>%
  rename(to = id) %>%
  filter(MainSubject == "Work related") %>%
  group_by(from, to) %>%
    summarise(weight = n()) %>%
  filter(from != to) %>%
  filter(weight > 1) %>%
  ungroup()

title: Hands-on Exercise 7-A:
text:
9.1 A full centrality scorecard
Instead of looking at betweenness alone, I compute five centrality measures with tidygraph and present them in a searchable, sortable DT table. This lets us identify who matters in the network from several angles at once.

centrality_tbl <- GAStech_graph %>%
  activate(nodes) %>%
  mutate(degree      = centrality_degree(mode = "all"),
         betweenness = centrality_betweenness(),
         closeness   = centrality_closeness(),
         eigen       = centrality_eigen(weights = NULL),
         pagerank    = centrality_pagerank()) %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  select(label, Department, Title,
         degree, betweenness, closeness, eigen, pagerank) %>%
  arrange(desc(betweenness))

datatable(centrality_tbl,
          filter = "top",
          caption = "Centrality scorecard for all 54 employees",
          options = list(pageLength = 10)) %>%
  formatRound(c("betweenness", "closeness", "eigen", "pagerank"), 3)











A high betweenness with a modest degree flags a broker — someone who bridges otherwise separate parts of the organisation.

title: Hands-on Exercise 7-A:
text:
9.2 Who are the top brokers?
I rank the 10 employees with the highest betweenness centrality and colour them by department. These are the people whose absence would most fragment internal communication.

top_brokers <- GAStech_graph %>%
  activate(nodes) %>%
  mutate(betweenness = centrality_betweenness()) %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  slice_max(betweenness, n = 10)

ggplot(top_brokers,
       aes(x = reorder(label, betweenness),
           y = betweenness,
           fill = Department)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Top 10 brokers by betweenness centrality",
       x = NULL, y = "Betweenness centrality") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Hands-on Exercise 7-A:
text:
9.3 Department-to-department communication heatmap
Networks can also be read as matrices. Here I aggregate the work-related emails by the sender’s and recipient’s department and draw a heatmap, revealing which departments talk to each other the most.

dept_matrix <- GAStech_edges %>%
  filter(MainSubject == "Work related") %>%
  left_join(GAStech_nodes %>% select(label, from_dept = group),
            by = c("sourceLabel" = "label")) %>%
  left_join(GAStech_nodes %>% select(label, to_dept = group),
            by = c("targetLabel" = "label")) %>%
  count(from_dept, to_dept, name = "messages")

ggplot(dept_matrix,
       aes(x = to_dept, y = from_dept, fill = messages)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = messages), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#fff7ec", high = "#b30000") +
  labs(title = "Work-email volume between departments",
       x = "Recipient department", y = "Sender department",
       fill = "Messages") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))














The strong diagonal confirms that most communication stays within departments, but the off-diagonal cells expose the cross-team channels.

title: Hands-on Exercise 7-A:
text:
9.4 Comparing community-detection algorithms
The guided exercise used edge-betweenness and optimal-modularity communities. Different algorithms can disagree, so I compare three popular methods on an undirected version of the graph and visualise each in a tabset.

# Collapse the directed graph into a *simple* undirected graph: the parallel
# A->B / B->A edges are merged and their Weights summed. This matters because
# cluster_fast_greedy() (and friends) reject multi-edges.
GAStech_undirected <- GAStech_graph %>%
  igraph::as_undirected(mode = "collapse",
                        edge.attr.comb = list(Weight = "sum", "ignore")) %>%
  as_tbl_graph()

plot_community <- function(graph, group_col, title) {
  graph %>%
    ggraph(layout = "fr") +
    geom_edge_link(aes(width = Weight), alpha = 0.15) +
    scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 4)) +
    geom_node_point(aes(colour = {{ group_col }}), size = 4) +
    labs(title = title, colour = "Community") +
    theme_graph()
}


LouvainInfomapFast-greedy



GAStech_undirected %>%
  mutate(community = as.factor(group_louvain(weights = Weight))) %>%
  plot_community(community, "Louvain communities")











GAStech_undirected %>%
  mutate(community = as.factor(group_infomap())) %>%
  plot_community(community, "Infomap communities")











GAStech_undirected %>%
  mutate(community = as.factor(group_fast_greedy(weights = Weight))) %>%
  plot_community(community, "Fast-greedy communities")











How many communities did each method find?

community_sizes <- tibble(
  Louvain      = GAStech_undirected %>% mutate(c = group_louvain(weights = Weight)) %>% pull(c) %>% n_distinct(),
  Infomap      = GAStech_undirected %>% mutate(c = group_infomap()) %>% pull(c) %>% n_distinct(),
  `Fast-greedy`= GAStech_undirected %>% mutate(c = group_fast_greedy(weights = Weight)) %>% pull(c) %>% n_distinct()
)
community_sizes

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  Louvain Infomap `Fast-greedy`
    <int>   <int>         <int>
1       4       6             4

title: Hands-on Exercise 7-A:
text:
9.5 An interactive dashboard + autosaved figure
Finally I build a richer visNetwork dashboard where node size encodes degree centrality, hovering shows a tooltip with the person’s title and department, and the user can filter by department or highlight a node’s neighbourhood. I also ggsave() a high-resolution static version to images/ so there is a saved image artefact on disk.

# degree of every node, in graph order
node_degree <- GAStech_graph %>%
  activate(nodes) %>%
  mutate(deg = centrality_degree(mode = "all")) %>%
  pull(deg)

vis_nodes <- GAStech_nodes %>%
  mutate(value = node_degree,
         title = paste0("<b>", label, "</b><br>",
                        "Title: ", Title, "<br>",
                        "Dept: ", group))

visNetwork(vis_nodes,
           GAStech_edges_aggregated,
           main = "GAStech work-email network — interactive dashboard") %>%
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr") %>%
  visEdges(arrows = "to",
           smooth = list(enabled = TRUE, type = "curvedCW"),
           color = list(opacity = 0.4)) %>%
  visOptions(highlightNearest = list(enabled = TRUE, degree = 1, hover = TRUE),
             nodesIdSelection = TRUE,
             selectedBy = "group") %>%
  visLegend() %>%
  visInteraction(navigationButtons = TRUE) %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 123)





A static, publication-quality version is rendered below and saved to disk with ggsave():

if (!dir.exists("images")) dir.create("images")

pub_plot <- GAStech_graph %>%
  mutate(betweenness = centrality_betweenness()) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = Weight), alpha = 0.15) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 4)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department, size = betweenness)) +
  scale_size(range = c(1, 9)) +
  labs(title = "GAStech work-email network",
       subtitle = "Node size = betweenness centrality",
       colour = "Department", size = "Betweenness") +
  theme_graph()

ggsave("images/HO_EX07A_network.png", pub_plot,
       width = 10, height = 8, dpi = 300, bg = "white")

pub_plot














On render, every figure in this document is also automatically written by knitr to the HO_EX07A_files/figure-html/ folder, and the dashboard figure above is explicitly saved to images/HO_EX07A_network.png.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5-D:
text:
Parallel coordinates plot is a data visualisation specially designed for visualising and analysing multivariate, numerical data. It is ideal for comparing multiple quantitative variables together and seeing the relationships between them. Its strength is that the variables can even be completely different: different ranges and even different units.
By the end of this hands-on exercise, I will gain hands-on experience on:

plotting statistic parallel coordinates plots by using ggparcoord() of GGally package, and
plotting interactive parallel coordinates plots by using parallelPlot package.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5-D:
text:
3.1 Plotting a simple parallel coordinates
The code chunk below plots a basic parallel coordinate plot.


Show the code

           columns = c(7:12)) +

  theme_minimal() +

      plot.title = element_text(hjust=0, face = "bold"),
      axis.title.x = element_blank(),
      axis.title.y = element_text(hjust=1, angle=0)
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis(n.dodge = 2))

title: Hands-on Exercise 5-D:
section: 3.3 Plotting a parallel coordinates with boxplot
text:
3.3 Plotting a parallel coordinates with boxplot
The basic parallel coordinates failed to reveal any meaning understanding of the World Happiness measures.

ggparcoord(data = wh, 
           columns = c(7:12), 
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE, 
           title = "Parallel Coordinates Plot of World Happines Variables")








Things to learn from the code chunk above.

groupColumn argument is used to group the observations (i.e. parallel lines) by using a single variable (i.e. Region) and colour the parallel coordinates lines by region name.
scale argument is used to scale the variables in the parallel coordinate plot by using uniminmax method. The method univariately scale each variable so the minimum of the variable is zero and the maximum is one.
alphaLines argument is used to reduce the intensity of the line colour to 0.2. The permissible value range is between 0 to 1.
boxplot argument is used to turn on the boxplot by using logical TRUE. The default is FALSE.
title argument is used to provide the parallel coordinates plot a title.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5-D:
text:
3.4 Parallel coordinates with facet
Since ggparcoord() is developed by extending ggplot2 package, we can combination use some of the ggplot2 function when plotting a parallel coordinates plot.
In the code chunk below, facet_wrap() of ggplot2 is used to plot 10 small multiple parallel coordinates plots. Each plot represent one geographical region such as East Asia.

ggparcoord(data = wh, 
           columns = c(7:12), 
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE, 
           title = "Multiple Parallel Coordinates Plots of World Happines Variables by Region") +
  facet_wrap(~ Region)

title: Hands-on Exercise 5-D:
text:
3.5 Parallel coordinates with palette
Viridis Color Palette groupColumn = "Region" groups and colours the observations by their Region. We apply scale_color_viridis_d() to ensure the color palette is accessible and visually distinct.


Show the code

           columns = c(7:12),
           groupColumn = "Region") +
  labs(title = "Basic Parallel Plot, grouped by Region") +

      axis.title.x = element_blank(),

      legend.text = element_text(size=8),
      legend.position = "bottom"
  ) +

  labs(title = "Basic Parallel Plot, highlighting a group") +

                              "#E8E8E8", "#E8E8E8", "#E8E8E8", "#E8E8E8", 
                              "#E8E8E8", "#69b3a2")) +

      legend.text = element_text(size=8),

title: Hands-on Exercise 5-D:
text:
3.7 Parallel coordinates with facet (2)
Since ggparcoord() is developed by extending ggplot2 package, we can combine it with some ggplot2 functions when plotting.
In the code chunk below, facet_wrap() of ggplot2 is used to plot 10 small multiple parallel coordinates plots. Each plot represents one geographical region.


Show the code
ggparcoord(data = wh, 
           columns = c(7:12), 
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE, 
           title = "Multiple Parallel Coordinates Plots by Region") +
  facet_wrap(~ Region, labeller = labeller(group = label_wrap_gen(width = 25))) +
  scale_color_viridis_d() +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
      plot.title = element_text(hjust=0, face = "bold"),

title: Hands-on Exercise 5-B:
text:
Correlation coefficient is a popular statistic that use to measure the type and strength of the relationship between two variables. The values of a correlation coefficient ranges between -1.0 and 1.0. A correlation coefficient of 1 shows a perfect linear relationship between the two variables, while a -1.0 shows a perfect inverse relationship between the two variables. A correlation coefficient of 0.0 shows no linear relationship between the two variables.
When multivariate data are used, the correlation coefficeints of the pair comparisons are displayed in a table form known as correlation matrix or scatterplot matrix.

First, we will learn how to create correlation matrix using pairs() of R Graphics.
Next, you will learn how to plot corrgram using corrplot package of R.
Lastly, you will learn how to create an interactive correlation matrix using plotly R.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5-B:
text:
3.1 Basic correlation matrix
Figure below shows the scatter plot matrix of Wine Quality Data. It is a 11x11 matrix.


Show the code
pairs(wine[,1:11],
      main = "Correlation Matrix")











Show the code
pairs(wine[,2:12])










3.2 Drawing the lower corner


Show the code
pairs(wine[,2:12], 
      upper.panel = NULL,
      main = "Correlation Matrix with Lower Panel")









The code chunk below displays the upper half of the correlation matrix.


Show the code
pairs(wine[,2:12], 
      lower.panel = NULL,
      main = "Correlation Matrix with Upper Panel")

title: Hands-on Exercise 5-B:
text:
3.3 Including Correlation Coefficients
To show the correlation coefficient of each pair of variables instead of a scatter plot, panel.cor function will be used. This will also show higher correlations in a larger font.


Show the code
panel.cor <- function(x, y, digits=2, prefix="", cex.cor, ...) {
usr <- par("usr")
on.exit(par(usr))
par(usr = c(0, 1, 0, 1))
r <- abs(cor(x, y, use="complete.obs"))
txt <- format(c(r, 0.123456789), digits=digits)[1]
txt <- paste(prefix, txt, sep="")
if(missing(cex.cor)) cex.cor <- 0.8/strwidth(txt)
text(0.5, 0.5, txt, cex = cex.cor * (1 + r) / 2)
}

pairs(wine[,2:12], 
      upper.panel = panel.cor,
      main = "Correlation Matrix with Correlation Coefficients")

title: Hands-on Exercise 5-B:
text:
6.3 Working with visual geometrics
In corrplot package, there are seven visual geometrics (parameter method) can be used to encode the attribute values. They are: circle, square, ellipse, number, shade, color and pie. The default is circle. As shown in the previous section, the default visual geometric of corrplot matrix is circle. However, this default setting can be changed by using the method argument as shown in the code chunk below.

corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "ellipse")

title: Hands-on Exercise 5-B:
text:
6.4 Working with layout
corrplor() supports three layout types, namely: “full”, “upper” or “lower”. The default is “full” which display full matrix. The default setting can be changed by using the type argument of corrplot().

corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "ellipse", 
         type="lower")








The default layout of the corrgram can be further customised. For example, arguments diag and tl.col are used to turn off the diagonal cells and to change the axis text label colour to black colour respectively as shown in the code chunk and figure below.

corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "ellipse", 
         type="lower",
         diag = FALSE,
         tl.col = "black")

title: Hands-on Exercise 5-B:
text:
6.5 Working with mixed layout
With corrplot package, it is possible to design corrgram with mixed visual matrix of one half and numerical matrix on the other half. In order to create a coorgram with mixed layout, the corrplot.mixed(), a wrapped function for mixed visualisation style will be used.
Figure below shows a mixed layout corrgram plotted using wine quality data.

corrplot.mixed(wine.cor, 
               lower = "ellipse", 
               upper = "number",
               tl.pos = "lt",
               diag = "l",
               tl.col = "black")








The code chunk used to plot the corrgram are shown below.

corrplot.mixed(wine.cor, 
               lower = "ellipse", 
               upper = "number",
               tl.pos = "lt",
               diag = "l",
               tl.col = "black")








Notice that argument lower and upper are used to define the visualisation method used. In this case ellipse is used to map the lower half of the corrgram and numerical matrix (i.e. number) is used to map the upper half of the corrgram. The argument tl.pos, on the other, is used to specify the placement of the axis label. Lastly, the diag argument is used to specify the glyph on the principal diagonal of the corrgram.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5-B:
section: 6.6 Combining corrgram with the significant test
text:
6.6 Combining corrgram with the significant test
In statistical analysis, we are also interested to know which pair of variables their correlation coefficients are statistically significant.
Figure below shows a corrgram combined with the significant test. The corrgram reveals that not all correlation pairs are statistically significant. For example the correlation between total sulfur dioxide and free surfur dioxide is statistically significant at significant level of 0.1 but not the pair between total sulfur dioxide and citric acid.
With corrplot package, we can use the cor.mtest() to compute the p-values and confidence interval for each pair of variables.

wine.sig = cor.mtest(wine.cor, conf.level= .95)

We can then use the p.mat argument of corrplot function as shown in the code chunk below.

corrplot(wine.cor,
         method = "number",
         type = "lower",
         diag = FALSE,
         tl.col = "black",
         tl.srt = 45,
         p.mat = wine.sig$p,
         sig.level = .05)

title: Hands-on Exercise 5-B:
text:
6.7 Reorder a corrgram
Matrix reorder is very important for mining the hiden structure and pattern in a corrgram. By default, the order of attributes of a corrgram is sorted according to the correlation matrix (i.e. “original”). The default setting can be over-write by using the order argument of corrplot(). Currently, corrplot package support four sorting methods, they are:

“AOE” is for the angular order of the eigenvectors. See Michael Friendly (2002) for details.
“FPC” for the first principal component order.
“hclust” for hierarchical clustering order, and “hclust.method” for the agglomeration method to be used.

“hclust.method” should be one of “ward”, “single”, “complete”, “average”, “mcquitty”, “median” or “centroid”.

“alphabet” for alphabetical order.

“AOE”, “FPC”, “hclust”, “alphabet”. More algorithms can be found in seriation package.

corrplot.mixed(wine.cor, 
               lower = "ellipse", 
               upper = "number",
               tl.pos = "lt",
               diag = "l",
               order="AOE",
               tl.col = "black")

title: Hands-on Exercise 5-B:
section: 6.8 Reordering a correlation matrix using hclust
text:
6.8 Reordering a correlation matrix using hclust
If using hclust, corrplot() can draw rectangles around the corrgram based on the results of hierarchical clustering. addrect= specifies number of clusters.


Show the code
corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "ellipse", 
         tl.pos = "lt",
         tl.col = "black",
         tl.srt = 45,
         tl.cex = 0.6,
         order="hclust",
         hclust.method = "ward.D",
         addrect = 3)

title: Hands-on Exercise 4-D:
text:
Funnel plot is a specially designed data visualisation for conducting unbiased comparison between outlets, stores or business entities. By the end of this hands-on exercise, you will gain hands-on experience on:

plotting funnel plots by using funnelPlotR package,
plotting static funnel plot by using ggplot2 package, and

In this exercise, four R packages will be used. They are:

FunnelPlotR for creating funnel plot.
ggplot2 for creating funnel plot manually.
knitr for building static html table.
plotly for creating interactive funnel plot.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4-D:
text:
4.1 Computing the basic derived fields
To plot the funnel plot from scratch, we need to derive cumulative death rate (rate) and standard error of cumulative death rate (rate.se).

df <- covid19 %>%
  mutate(rate = Death / Positive) %>%
  mutate(rate.se = sqrt((rate*(1-rate)) / (Positive))) %>%
  filter(rate > 0)

Next, the fit.mean is computed by using the code chunk below.
The function calculates the weighted mean of the rate column in the df data frame, where the weights are the inverse squares of the corresponding standard errors (rate.se).

fit.mean <- weighted.mean(df$rate, 1/df$rate.se^2)
fit.mean

[1] 0.01496959

title: Hands-on Exercise 4-D:
section: 4.2 Calculate lower and upper limits for 95% and 99.9% CI
text:
4.2 Calculate lower and upper limits for 95% and 99.9% CI
The code chunk below is used to compute the lower and upper limits for 95% confidence interval.
The number.seq creates a sequence of numbers from 1 to the maximum number of positive cases in the data frame (max = 6231).
We then calculate the lower and upper 95% confidence intervals and the lower and upper 99.9% confidence intervals for the mean rate of death at each number in the sequence.
Finally, a new data frame dfCI is created that contains the lower and upper confidence intervals and mean rate of death for each number in the sequence.


Show the code
number.seq <- seq(1, max(df$Positive), 1)
number.ll95 <- fit.mean - 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
number.ul95 <- fit.mean + 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
number.ll999 <- fit.mean - 3.29 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
number.ul999 <- fit.mean + 3.29 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
dfCI <- data.frame(number.ll95, number.ul95, number.ll999, 
                   number.ul999, number.seq, fit.mean)
