title: Hands-on Exercise 9C:
text:
This hands-on exercise covers Chapter 23: Analytical Mapping.
Analytical mapping goes beyond pretty choropleths toward spatial exploratory data analysis (ESDA). In this exercise I:

Import an rds polygon layer of Nigeria water points by LGA.
Map rates (proportions) rather than raw counts.
Build percentile maps and box maps to surface spatial outliers.
Write reusable functions (get.var, percentmap, boxbreaks, boxmap).

title: Hands-on Exercise 9C:
text:
Percentile map
Special quantile map with six categories: 0–1%, 1–10%, 10–50%, 50–90%, 90–99%, 99–100%.

NGA_wp <- NGA_wp %>% drop_na()

get.var <- function(vname, df) {
  v <- df[vname] %>% st_set_geometry(NULL)
  v <- unname(v[, 1])
  return(v)
}

percentmap <- function(vnam, df, legtitle = NA, mtitle = "Percentile Map") {
  percent <- c(0, .01, .1, .5, .9, .99, 1)
  var <- get.var(vnam, df)
  bperc <- quantile(var, percent)
  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons() +
    tm_shape(df) +
    tm_fill(vnam, title = legtitle, breaks = bperc, palette = "Blues",
            labels = c("< 1%", "1% - 10%", "10% - 50%",
                       "50% - 90%", "90% - 99%", "> 99%")) +
    tm_borders() +
    tm_title(mtitle) +
    tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE)
}

percentmap("total_wp", NGA_wp)

title: Hands-on Exercise 9C:
Hands-on Exercise 9C:
section: Counts vs rates, side by side (proving the point)
text:
Counts vs rates, side by side (proving the point)
The chapter asserts that counts mislead. Here I show it: the same LGAs that look “worst” by raw non-functional count are different from those worst by non-functional rate.

count_map <- boxmap("wp_nonfunctional", NGA_wp,
                    mtitle = "Box map: non-functional COUNT")
rate_map  <- boxmap("pct_nonfunctional", NGA_wp,
                    mtitle = "Box map: non-functional RATE")
tmap_arrange(count_map, rate_map, ncol = 2)














TipInsight



Large, populous LGAs dominate the count map simply because they have more of everything. The rate map re-ranks small LGAs where most water points are broken, which are the genuine service-failure hotspots.

Generalising percentile/box maps over many variables
The functions take the variable name as a string, so I can loop them across a vector of variables instead of copy-pasting.

box_maps <- lapply(vars, function(v) boxmap(v, NGA_wp, mtitle = v))

NGA_valid <- st_make_valid(NGA_wp)

title: Chart Whisperer
section: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
Mythbusting Risk Stereotypes in Motor Insurance
Method: 10 mythbusting research questions, tidyverse data wrangling, and best-fit ggplot visual analytics

I am framing this presentation as a mythbusting investigation of motor insurance risk. Instead of assuming common stereotypes are true, I test them against portfolio data from 2022 to 2024. I focus on loss ratio, claim frequency, claim severity, underwriting result, exposure, and retention because these measures show whether a segment is actually profitable, risky, or worth protecting.

title: Chart Whisperer
text:
Executive Summary
The portfolio is profitable overall, but profitability is uneven.








Strategic objective
Main finding
Business action


Profitability
Comprehensive without excess and very short-exposure policies create the clearest pressure.
Review excess design, short-duration loading, and claims controls.


Retention
Customers observed all 3 years are materially more profitable than one-year customers.
Protect low-risk loyal customers from blunt repricing.


Calibrated pricing
Some stereotypes are real, but many are mixed.
Price using frequency, severity, materiality, and evidence together.




My overall message is that the portfolio is profitable, but the profitability is uneven. I want to show that stereotypes can be useful starting hypotheses, but they should not become pricing rules by themselves. The clearest actions are to review comprehensive without excess, monitor very short-exposure policies, retain profitable loyal customers, and use age, brand, vehicle value, and geography as calibrated supporting signals.

title: Chart Whisperer
text:
Contents

Executive summary and objectives
Methodology, data, and technique rationale
Portfolio trend and policy-type triage
Mythbusting findings by risk dimension
Answers to the 10 research questions
Recommendations


I will first explain the objective, data preparation, and technique choices, then move into the key visual findings. The flow is designed to move from overall portfolio performance into segment-level mythbusting. I end by answering the 10 research questions and linking the evidence back to profitability, retention, and calibrated pricing.

Here I am showing how the analysis is made reproducible. The sandbox starts from the raw CSV and Excel dictionary, then derives loss ratio, frequency, severity, exposure bands, age bands, loyalty, brand tier, and geography. I also match each visual technique to a decision need: tiles summarise KPI pressure, half-eye plots show distribution overlap, ridgelines show tail risk, and heatmaps reveal interaction effects.

title: Chart Whisperer
text:
One-Look Portfolio Trend


This slide gives the portfolio-level baseline before I discuss segments. I use a static dashboard so premium, incurred loss, underwriting result, loss ratio, and claim frequency can be compared at once. The main pattern I want the audience to see is whether deterioration is driven by profitability, claim activity, or portfolio scale, rather than treating the loss ratio as a standalone number.

title: Chart Whisperer
text:
Policy-Type Triage


This slide is my first prioritisation view. I compare policy type across loss ratio, claim frequency, claim severity, and premium share. The important point is that not every weak segment needs the same response. A high-frequency segment suggests product, deductible, or renewal controls, while a high-severity segment suggests reserve, claims, or coverage review.

title: Chart Whisperer
text:
Profitability Status


Here I break each policy type into no-claim, claim-but-profitable, and loss-making records. This helps me show whether a product problem is broad-based or concentrated in a loss-making tail. The key interpretation is that comprehensive without excess should be treated as a frequency-management concern, and we should not assume that higher cover automatically means stronger profitability.

title: Chart Whisperer
text:
Bonus Score Signal


This slide tests whether bonus score cleanly separates good and bad risks. The half-eye plot shows the shape and overlap of the loss-ratio distributions, while the boxplot summarises the central spread. My interpretation is that bonus score is directionally useful, especially for frequency, but the overlap means it should support pricing rather than act as a single blunt rule.

title: Chart Whisperer
text:
Exposure Duration and Loyalty


This slide connects two strategic questions: early-duration risk and customer loyalty. On the left, I use ridgelines to check whether short-exposure policies have a heavier adverse loss-ratio distribution. On the right, I compare premium share and loss ratio by observed customer duration. The pattern supports monitoring short-exposure policies while protecting longer-observed customers that show stronger profitability.

title: Chart Whisperer
text:
Cancellation Quality


Here I explain why cancellation should not be interpreted too casually. If high-risk policies cancel, attrition may reduce pressure, but if profitable customers leave, retention quality worsens. I use the bonus-score split to show whether weaker risks are actually leaving. My main takeaway is that the insurer should detect poor risks earlier instead of relying on cancellation to clean the portfolio.

title: Chart Whisperer
text:
Driver and Vehicle Interaction


This heatmap shows why I include multivariate analysis. Looking only at driver age or vehicle age separately can hide important combinations. Each cell shows claim frequency for a driver-age and vehicle-age pairing. The cells with higher frequency indicate where pricing interactions or underwriting rules may be more useful than a simple age-only or vehicle-age-only adjustment.

title: Chart Whisperer
text:
Brand, Value, and Geography


This slide tests three common status and location stereotypes. I use point intervals for brand severity because uncertainty matters, and tile views for vehicle value and geography so the loss-ratio differences are easy to compare. My interpretation is that these variables are useful supporting lenses, but they should lead to calibrated loadings, not automatic surcharges.

title: Chart Whisperer
text:
Answers to the 10 Research Questions










RQ
Verdict
Answer




RQ1
Mixed
18-25 has highest frequency (0.488) but only 62.5% LR; worst age LR is 26-35.


RQ2
Partly real
0-3 vehicles claim most often (0.524), but worst LR is 13-20 (75.2%).


RQ3
Busted
Comprehensive without excess has 93.9% LR and 1.046 frequency.


RQ4
Mostly busted
Premium brands have higher frequency but lower LR (68.9%) than mainstream brands (70.7%).


RQ5
Mixed
Highest-value LR is 73.3%, but lowest-value LR is also weak at 72.3%.


RQ6
Mostly real
Bad has highest frequency (0.624); Neutral has highest LR (81.4%).


RQ7
Busted
Very short exposure is above break-even at 103.3% LR.


RQ8
Busted
Observed all 3 years has best LR (63.4%) versus one-year customers (88.2%).


RQ9
Real
Cancelled policies are worse: 128.0% LR versus active 64.4%.


RQ10
Mixed
Urban has higher frequency and LR; rural has higher severity (995.91).






This slide summarises the 10 research questions as evidence-backed verdicts. I use “mixed”, “busted”, or “real” to make the conclusions easy to follow. The important point is that a stereotype may be true for frequency but false for overall profitability, so I interpret each myth using loss ratio, frequency, severity, materiality, and loyalty evidence together.

title: Chart Whisperer
text:
Recommendations

Retain longer-observed customers with strong profitability.
Review comprehensive without excess and very short-exposure policies first.
Detect cancellation-prone poor risks earlier, before losses emerge.
Use age, brand, vehicle value, and geography as calibrated signals, not stereotypes.
Treat the priority queue as a review list, not as a pricing model.


I close by translating the visual findings into actions. For profitability, I would review comprehensive without excess and very short-exposure policies first. For retention, I would protect longer-observed profitable customers. For pricing, I would use the mythbusting evidence to calibrate age, brand, value, geography, and cancellation signals instead of applying broad stereotype-based rules.

title: Take-home Exercise 2:
text:
This report answers VAST Challenge 2026 Mini-Challenge 1. All main graphs are interactive: hover over points, tiles, nodes or bars to view tooltips with the underlying details.


TenantThread is being acquired by CivicLoom Realty Partners under an embargo until 6:00 PM on 2046-06-05. Seven AI agents manage communications, with a compliance agent (“The Judge”) assigned to enforce the rules. Despite that guardrail, merger details appeared on agent-linked social accounts around 5:00 PM, roughly one hour early.





What were the key events and relationships that led up to the inappropriate release? Visualise the sequence of events (key actions, causal relationships, decision points and actors), and highlight what let the post past embargo enforcement.
The evasion of the embargo was a new behaviour. Discover and illustrate the typical behaviour of the agents, and compare it to the behaviour that led to the release.
Were there leading indicators that such a release was possible? Did agents’ actual behaviour ever differ from their expected behaviour, and why did earlier occasions draw no action?











NoteApproach



I flatten the nested JSON into message- and round-level tables, then combine timelines, channel and network views, baseline comparisons, and anomaly framing to explain how the embargo breach unfolded.

title: Take-home Exercise 2:
text:
3.1 Data quality & caveats
The file has a few inconsistencies that affect parsing or display. They are handled up front; none changes the headline findings.








#
Issue
Handling




1
Schema mismatch. The shipped mc1 data description.md describes an agent_outputs / declared_action-per-agent structure that does not match the delivered JSON (rounds[] → {hour, environment_context, communications[], participants[]}, with private reasoning in free-text internal_state).
Wrangle against the actual file.


2
Recipient identifier inconsistency. The social agent is social_media as a sender (agent_role) but social_manager as a recipient token. A naive join on role silently drops every edge to Social-Mgr (incl. the largest, Legal→Social-Mgr = 52).
Map recipient tokens → agents with an explicit table (Fig 6).


3
Stock $180 artifact at 11:00 - a 6× spike wedged between NAs during a CRITICAL collapse, almost certainly a data-entry error.
Excluded; shown three ways in Fig 1 so the reader can judge.


4
Crisis-day stock ~50% missing - no price reported at 09–11h or 16–18h.
Line breaks across the gaps; the complete sentiment strip carries the crisis window.


5
Two sentiment labelling schemes - lowercase pre-crisis (neutral…critical) vs UPPERCASE crisis-day (LOW/CRITICAL/RECOVERING) give 7 levels, two sharing a colour.
Harmonized to 5 ordered levels (one calm→crisis→recovery ramp).



The nested JSON is flattened into messages (one row per communication) and rounds (one row per hour).

Each communication becomes one row, including the three internal_state reasoning fields.


Show the code
`%or%` <- function(a, b) if (is.null(a) || length(a) == 0) b else a

hours    <- map_chr(rounds_raw, "hour")
is_crisis <- str_starts(hours, "2046-06-05")   # crisis day = hourly 2046-06-05 rounds

messages <- imap(rounds_raw, function(rd, i) {
  map(rd$communications, function(c) {
    ist <- c$internal_state %or% list()
    tibble(
      round_idx     = i - 1L,

      agent_id      = gc(c, "agent_id"),
      agent_role    = gc(c, "agent_role"),
      channel       = gc(c, "channel"),
      message_type  = gc(c, "message_type"),
      responding_to = gc(c, "responding_to"),
      recipients    = paste(unlist(c$recipients %or% list()), collapse = "; "),
      content       = gc(c, "content"),
      reacting      = ist$reacting      %or% NA_character_,
      rationalizing = ist$rationalizing %or% NA_character_,
      deliberating  = ist$deliberating  %or% NA_character_

3.3 Deriving the behavioural fields
Key derived fields mark phase, public/unofficial-public channel use, deal mentions and seniority.

  mutate(
    phase = if_else(as_date(hour) == as_date("2046-06-05"), "crisis", "pre-crisis"),
    channel = factor(channel, chan_levels),

title: Take-home Exercise 2:
text:
5.1 Escalation timeline






NoteHandling a data artifact, transparently



The crisis-day stock series contains an isolated $180 at 11:00, surrounded by missing values during a CRITICAL-sentiment collapse. I treat it as a data artifact, but show three views so the choice is auditable.




Show the shared timeline builder
events <- tribble(
  ~round_idx, ~label,
  3,  "Shadow channel\nactivated",   8,  "@Elena leak →\nJudge deployed",
  10, "SaltWind #1",                 12, "SaltWind #2\n(eve of crisis)",
  21, "5 PM BREACH\n(personal/anon posts)", 22, "6 PM embargo\nlift")
# Harmonize the dataset's two sentiment label schemes into one ordered scale (see `aes`).
rr <- rounds |>
  mutate(sentiment = factor(sent_recode[sentiment], sent5_lv),
         tick = if_else(phase=="crisis", format(hour, "%Hh"), format(hour, "%b %d")))

# Rich timeline: sentiment strip + stock line + event annotations.
# `stock_col` chooses which stock column to draw; keeps the three tabs DRY.
build_timeline <- function(df, stock_col, cap) {
  df <- df |> mutate(
    tip_sent  = paste0(tick, " - sentiment: ", sentiment),
    tip_stock = paste0(tick, " - $", .data[[stock_col]], " · ", sentiment, "\n", str_trunc(headline, 55)))
  ggplot(df, aes(round_idx)) +
    geom_tile_interactive(aes(y = 15, fill = sentiment, tooltip = tip_sent, data_id = round_idx),
                          height = 2.4, width = 0.95) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = sent5_col, name = "Market sentiment", drop = FALSE,
                      guide = guide_legend(nrow = 1)) +
    geom_line(aes(y = .data[[stock_col]]), colour = OI[["blue"]], linewidth = 1) +
    geom_point_interactive(aes(y = .data[[stock_col]], tooltip = tip_stock, data_id = round_idx),
                           colour = OI[["blue"]], size = 2) +
    annotate("rect", xmin = 12.5, xmax = 22.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = OI[["red"]], alpha = 0.05) +
    annotate("text", x = 15, y = 44, label = "crisis day (hourly)", colour = OI[["red"]],
             size = 3.2, fontface = "italic", hjust = 0.5) +
    geom_vline(data = events, aes(xintercept = round_idx), linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey40") +
    geom_label(data = events, aes(x = round_idx, y = c(40,37,41,37,29,43), label = label),
               size = 2.7, fill = "white", label.size = 0, lineheight = 0.9, colour = "grey15") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = rr$round_idx, labels = rr$tick, expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.08))) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(13.5, 45), breaks = c(20,30,40), labels = dollar) +
    labs(title = "Fig 1 - TenantThread stock and market sentiment, May 17 to the crisis day",
         x = NULL, y = "Stock price", caption = cap) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7.5))
}


The timeline shows a two-week slide from $38.70 to about $27, followed by the 5 PM early confirmation.

Excluding artifact (A)Including artifact (B)Sentiment-led (C)

p1 <- build_timeline(rr_excl, "stock_excl",
        cap = "Sentiment uses one harmonized scale. No price reported 09–11h & 16–18h; the $180 outlier (11h) is excluded as a data artifact.")

title: Take-home Exercise 2:
text:
6.1 The interaction network
Pre-crisis, the delivered recipients field has no explicit directed private-recipient edges. On the crisis day, a senior off-record back-channel appears.

Tip: hover over any node to read that agent’s message frequency (total messages sent).


Network (node-link)Who-messages-whom (matrix)




Show the code
# recipient tokens are agent ROLES, but the social token is "social_manager" while the sender's
# agent_role is "social_media" - so map recipient tokens to agent_id explicitly (not via agent_role).
role_map <- tibble(
  recipients = c("legal","platform_trust","social_manager","pr","intern","pr_intern","judge"),
  to         = c("legal_agent","quality_agent","social_media_agent","pr_agent",
                 "intern_agent","pr_intern_agent","judge_agent"))
node_lab <- c(legal_agent="Legal", quality_agent="Plat-Trust", social_media_agent="Social-Mgr",
              pr_agent="PR", pr_intern_agent="PR-Intern", intern_agent="Intern", judge_agent="Judge")

# circular layout shared by both phase panels
k <- length(agent_levels)
nodes_xy <- tibble(agent_id = agent_levels,
                   ang = pi/2 + 2*pi*(seq_len(k) - 1)/k, x = cos(ang), y = sin(ang))

# node size = messages sent (transaction frequency), crisis day only
nodes <- tibble(agent_id = agent_levels) |>
  left_join(messages |> filter(phase == "crisis") |> count(agent_id, name = "sent"), by = "agent_id") |>
  left_join(nodes_xy, by = "agent_id") |>
  mutate(sent = coalesce(sent, 0L), lab = node_lab[agent_id])

# directed crisis-day edges: split recipients, drop ALL broadcasts, map role -> recipient agent
edges <- messages |> filter(phase == "crisis") |>
  transmute(from = agent_id, channel, recipients) |>
  separate_rows(recipients, sep = "; ") |>
  filter(recipients != "", recipients != "ALL") |>
  left_join(role_map, by = "recipients") |>
  filter(!is.na(to), to != from) |>
  group_by(from, to) |>
  summarise(n = n(), n_off = sum(channel == "side_huddle"), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(edge_type = if_else(n_off >= n/2, "off-record (side_huddle)", "other internal")) |>
  left_join(nodes_xy |> select(from = agent_id, x, y), by = "from") |>
  left_join(nodes_xy |> select(to = agent_id, xend = x, yend = y), by = "to")

p5 <- ggplot() +
  geom_curve(data = edges, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend, linewidth = n, colour = edge_type),
             curvature = 0.18, alpha = 0.65, lineend = "round",
             arrow = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(5, "pt"), type = "closed")) +
  geom_point_interactive(data = nodes, aes(x, y, size = sent, data_id = agent_id,
                         tooltip = paste0(lab, " - ", sent, " messages sent")),
                         colour = OI[["blue"]], alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_text(data = nodes, aes(x * 1.28, y * 1.28, label = lab), size = 3, colour = "grey15") +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 16, name = "messages sent") +
  scale_linewidth(range = c(0.3, 3.4), name = "msgs on edge") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("off-record (side_huddle)" = OI[["red"]],
                                 "other internal" = OI[["sky"]]), name = NULL) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-1.6, 1.6), ylim = c(-1.45, 1.45), clip = "off") +
  labs(title = "Fig 6 - Agent interaction network (crisis day)",
       caption = "Node size = messages sent (hover a node for its total); edge width = count; red = off-record side_huddle. ALL broadcasts excluded.") +
  theme_void(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
        plot.caption = element_text(size = 8.5, colour = "grey45", hjust = 0))
ggsave("figures/fig6_network.png", p5, width = 10.5, height = 6.5, dpi = 150, bg = "white")
show_girafe(p5, h = 6.5)








Figure 8

adj <- messages |> filter(phase == "crisis") |>
  transmute(from = agent_id, recipients) |>

  filter(recipients != "") |>
  left_join(role_map, by = "recipients") |>
  mutate(to_lab = if_else(recipients == "ALL", "ALL", agent_short[to])) |>
  count(from, to_lab, name = "n") |>

         to_f   = factor(to_lab, to_levels))

p5m <- ggplot(adj, aes(to_f, from_f, fill = n)) +
  geom_tile_interactive(aes(tooltip = paste0(from_f, " to ", to_f, ": ", n, " messages"),
                            data_id = paste(from_f, to_f)), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +

            colour = ifelse(pmin(adj$n, 40) > 24, "white", "grey15")) +

text:
7.1 A within-agent anomaly signal
Against each agent’s own baseline, Legal, Social-Mgr and PR-Intern exceed z > 2 as the crisis opens, while Platform-Trust and the Judge go quiet.


Show the code
vol <- messages |> count(round_idx, agent_id, name = "n") |>
  complete(round_idx = 0:22, agent_id = agent_levels, fill = list(n = 0L))
base <- vol |> filter(round_idx <= 12) |> group_by(agent_id) |>
  summarise(mu = mean(n), sd = sd(n), .groups = "drop")
tickv <- rounds |> transmute(round_idx,
           tick = if_else(phase == "crisis", format(hour, "%Hh"), format(hour, "%b %d"))) |>
  arrange(round_idx) |> pull(tick)
zdf <- vol |> left_join(base, by = "agent_id") |>
  mutate(z = if_else(sd > 0, (n - mu) / sd, NA_real_),
         agent_f = factor(agent_id, rev(agent_levels)),
         flag = !is.na(z) & z > 2,
         tip = paste0(agent_short[agent_id], " @ ", tickv[round_idx + 1], ": ", n,
                      " msgs (z = ", round(z, 1), " vs baseline)"))

p9 <- ggplot(zdf, aes(factor(round_idx, levels = 0:22), agent_f, fill = z)) +
  geom_tile_interactive(aes(tooltip = tip, data_id = paste(agent_f, round_idx)),
                        colour = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(data = filter(zdf, flag), shape = 4, size = 1.9, stroke = 0.9, colour = "grey10") +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 13.5, xmax = 23.5, ymin = 0.4, ymax = 7.6,
           fill = NA, colour = OI[["red"]], linewidth = 0.7, linetype = "longdash") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = OI[["blue"]], mid = "white", high = OI[["red"]], midpoint = 0,
                       na.value = "grey92", name = "z vs own baseline",
                       limits = c(-3, 6), oob = scales::squish) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = tickv) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = agent_short) +
  labs(title = "Fig 9 - Each agent vs its own pre-crisis baseline (z-score of message volume)",
       x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = "z = (round count - agent's pre-crisis mean) / sd; × marks z > 2; dashed box = crisis day. Hourly crisis rounds vs daily pre-crisis, so read z as a within-agent directional signal, not a p-value.") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7.5), panel.grid = element_blank())
ggsave("figures/fig9_zscore.png", p9, width = 11, height = 4.4, dpi = 150, bg = "white")
show_girafe(p9, h = 4.4)

title: Take-home Exercise 2:
section: 9.1 Q1 - Events, relationships and enforcement bypass
text:
9.1 Q1 - Events, relationships and enforcement bypass
Figures 1-4 show a pressure sequence: SaltWind exposes weakened sentiment and stock price, CivicLoom’s MAC risk became salient, and Legal shifted from containment to acceleration. At 16:00, Legal prepared a bilateral release trigger; at 17:00, after SaltWind reported merger talks, Legal claimed verbal CivicLoom consent and issued “GO”. The breach was not the held official release. It was the early confirmation by Legal-Agent and Social-Manager-Agent on personal/anonymous channels.
The core relationship is Legal plus Social-Mgr, supported by Platform-Trust and PR in the senior side-huddle. PR-Intern and Intern staged execution but did not make the decisive public posts. Enforcement failed because the posts used channels outside official-post review, after the Judge’s 15:00 hard stop and with no observed Judge action during 16:00-18:00.

title: Take-home Exercise 2:
section: 9.2 Q2 - Typical behaviour versus the anomalous release
text:
9.2 Q2 - Typical behaviour versus the anomalous release
Baseline behaviour is stable and role-bound. Across the 13 pre-crisis rounds, Legal and Platform-Trust act as internal advisers; Legal has 0 personal and 0 anonymous posts, and nobody uses anonymous_post. On the crisis day, Legal moves to 4 personal + 12 anonymous posts, while Social-Mgr reaches 14 personal posts. All anonymous posts in the dataset are crisis-day Legal posts.
The heatmap and network views show a categorical break. Legal enters a new public channel class and also becomes a high-volume private coordinator. The evasion was new behaviour because senior internal agents used unofficial-public channels and prepared the release through a private coordination structure.

title: Take-home Exercise 2:
text:
9.3 Q3 - Leading indicators
Yes. The clearest warning is the 2046-05-29 @Elena incident: Social-Mgr used a personal account to hint at CivicLoom news, a CivicLoom account engaged, and a reporter captured it before deletion. This is the same failure mode as the final breach: embargo-relevant information surfaced through an unofficial personal channel. Other indicators include the 2046-05-22 shadow channel, Legal’s unilateral freezes and crisis-day awareness of oversight gaps.
The indicators did not trigger effective action because they were treated as contained or routine. Deleting the @Elena post led to Judge deployment, but not to structural control over personal/anonymous channels. The system watched official statements while leaving the eventual breach channel open.
